relations.reason: The tenancy allegations and requested declaration in the identified plaint provide the pleaded context for the Supreme Court's characterization of the principal subject. This supports the characterization of the controversy, not the factual existence or validity of the asserted tenancy.
The opposing asserted durations demonstrate why the tenancy period is materially disputed. Neither asserted duration supplies proof that the claimed term existed.

The trial court's assessment that no cause of action was disclosed and that a statutory bar required rejection stands in procedural opposition to the Supreme Court's identification of a separate civil-adjudicable tenancy controversy. This is opposition between legal assessments at different court levels, not conflicting proof of the underlying tenancy facts.
The plaintiffs alleged forcible eviction, whereas the respondent trust denied forcible eviction and asserted lawful possession-taking. Both remain attributed party positions.

The plaintiffs' allegation supplies the affirmative asserted account underlying the contested nonconsensual, unlawful dispossession proposition. It is assertion-level support only, not independent evidence establishing that proposition.

The trust's contrary account opposes the allegation that the identified plaintiffs were dispossessed outside due process. The assertion of lawful taking does not independently establish consent, actual surrender or compliance with legal process.

The alleged surrendering tenants are not identified. Their possible overlap with the plaintiffs is unresolved, so the group-level surrender submission cannot be transferred to the particular plaintiffs or treated as proof that the disputed dispossession was consensual.

The Court identified the trial injunction's operative period as relevant to the possession dispute, but the necessary dates and their relationship to the alleged taking are absent. The timing observation leaves the full unlawful-dispossession proposition unresolved.

The judgment distinguishes settled possession from fugitive possession but does not establish these plaintiffs' settled possession. That missing merits determination prevents use of the abstract possession-protection principle as proof that the complete disputed dispossession proposition occurred.

The disputed possession event does not determine equitable entitlement to an injunction. Even potential restoration under Section 6 is analytically distinct from an injunction against a true owner; the necessary injunction-specific factual and discretionary assessment is uncompleted.

Alleged failure to comply with deposit directions, arrears and litigation conduct could be raised where legally relevant, but they remain trust-side assertions. Without established facts and a discretionary merits assessment, they cannot establish or defeat injunction entitlement.

coverage_limits: This is a source-constrained reconstruction for case 1841885, Sopan Sukhdeo Sable and others, at the fixed stage SUPREME_COURT_PLAINT_REJECTION_REVIEW. It is not a pre-judgment prediction, qualified legal approval or human gold standard.

The complete supplied Supreme Court judgment and supplied rule registry are the only materials used. References to other cases, statutes, pleadings, earlier orders, counsel submissions and possible documents reflect the judgment's account, not independent examination of those materials. No external law or research has been added.

The relevant procedural sequence is that the trial court rejected the plaint, the first appellate court affirmed in Regular Civil Appeal No.178 of 2000, and the High Court upheld the lower-court conclusions in second appeal. These decisions must retain their respective court levels and procedural stages; they do not establish the tenancy or possession merits.

Rule R1 requires meaningful screening of the whole plaint under Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d), using material factual averments rather than defence denials. Prayers for relief are distinct from the facts constituting a cause of action. A genuinely illusory cause, omission of necessary material facts or an apparent statutory bar still requires genuine judicial assessment; the screening method cannot be reduced to a mechanical checklist.

Rules R2 and R3 preserve separate subject matters. The Supreme Court characterized tenancy continuance, tenancy terms and tenancy duration as matters for civil adjudication. A genuine inquiry into alleged trust misconduct follows the Section 50 route, and the judgment describes Section 51 prior consent for suits of the kind specified in Section 50. Tenant status alone does not make a person interested in the trust for that provision. The record does not establish that consent was sought or absent.

Rule R4 does not treat the inclusion of a separate trust-inquiry prayer as independently sufficient to reject the entire plaint. Order VII Rule 11 does not authorize partial rejection of a plaint; striking out pleadings under Order VI Rule 16 is distinct. Order II Rules 1 and 2 concern complete claims and consequences of omitted or relinquished claims. No completed relinquishment application is established by the supplied judgment.

The eleven-year tenancy asserted by the plaintiffs and eleven-month tenancy asserted by the trust remain competing claims concerning one disputed tenancy arrangement. The plaintiffs' actual tenancy status, the correct tenancy duration, the existence and effect of any lease documentation and the continuance of tenancy on any relevant date are not established by the procedural decision.

Rules R5 and R6 maintain the distinction between the fact that opposing allegations were recorded and the truth of the underlying possession event. The plaintiffs alleged forcible eviction; the trust denied it and asserted lawful taking. The Supreme Court left the question to the trial court if raised and relevant. Neither unlawful dispossession nor voluntary surrender by these plaintiffs is established, and non-proof is not proof of falsity.

The trust-side description of surrender by most tenants and the separately recorded assertion that 22 out of 44 tenants surrendered are not reconciled. The identities of the allegedly surrendering tenants, their overlap with the plaintiffs, relevant dates and supporting evidence are unavailable. The trial court injunction's operative chronology is likewise unresolved.

Section 6 recovery for dispossession without consent otherwise than in due course of law is distinct from discretionary injunction relief. The supplied judgment recounts protection of settled possession and restrictions on injunctions against true owners in favor of unlawful possessors. It does not find that these plaintiffs were settled possessors, trespassers or unlawful possessors, does not determine the trust's true-owner status for the specific injunction issue and does not adjudicate the plaintiffs' equitable injunction entitlement.

The respondent trust's allegations concerning clean hands, Article 226 proceedings, noncompliance with earlier High Court deposit directions, arrears and surrender remain attributed contentions unless the judgment expressly records an actual finding. Their evidentiary significance is not supplied. The Supreme Court left relevant issues for trial and allowed the trust to seek directions concerning arrears where available in law.

The trust also submitted that only the District Court had jurisdiction rather than the court where the suit was filed. The Supreme Court expressly declined to express an opinion because the objection had not been specifically urged below. The lower courts' Section 80 reasoning and the Supreme Court's express Sections 50/51 analysis do not justify an invented general resolution of every possible Section 80 or exclusive-forum objection.

The rule registry contains OPEN_TEXT semantic evaluations that remain unimplemented: meaningful whole-plaint characterization, sufficiency of pleaded material facts, identification of a real tenancy subject rather than clever drafting, effect of competing tenancy terms, assessment of settled possession and actual possessors, consent and due process, relevance of possession dates and prior injunction orders, and discretionary injunction factors including ownership, lawful possession, prima facie case, balance of convenience and conduct. No applicable evidentiary burden has been supplied.

For disposition comparison only, the Supreme Court held the whole-plaint rejection unjustified, restricted further adjudication to tenancy, its terms and its period, permitted the plaintiffs one month to apply as warranted by law concerning relinquishment of other reliefs, and encouraged completion of trial within six months. The appeal was allowed to that extent without costs. None of these disposition directions is used as a factual antecedent proving tenancy validity, forcible dispossession, Section 6 recovery or injunction entitlement.
